THE DEEP RETURN
By ROBERT GIBSON

The oceanic research vessel Meridian set itself grimly to meet the approaching anomaly with defensive protocols, determined to protect the surface world. But they erred in thinking the Deep Ones were too primitive to be strategic.

In the last hours, the sonar readings had grown stronger by many magnitudes, and had changed their signature from scattered interference through white noise to a coherent pattern of organized movement. That was the acoustic effect as the mass's velocity changed relative to the Meridian, as for forty hours the vessel had maintained position above the trench.

They had monitored many such signals come and go from the abyss's impenetrable depths, and had seen them fade, distort and disappear as the Meridian continued its research mission, driven by scientific curiosity toward understanding the planet's last unexplored frontier, leaving behind the mystery of yet another unidentified biological signature unaccompanied by visual confirmation where researchers might observe. They had grown familiar with the sight of wonders—of bioluminescent colonies spanning kilometers, of thermal vents that sustained ecosystems in perpetual darkness.

But now unprecedented excitement possessed the hundred-odd members of the Meridian's crew. It was a subdued excitement; men and women, they came and stood quietly gazing into the large sonar displays that showed the ascending formation, and there were young researchers who had been born after the Deep Surveys began and had never seen anything like this. The experienced scientists talked in low voices, in tones of mingled eagerness and apprehension, of what might lie at this mission's culmination. For the Meridian was witnessing history; the signals ahead were from the Bathys, whose existence had shaped their careers' beginning.

Dr. Omar Ward, the Meridian's director, came slowly down the narrow stair from the observation deck, into the large operations center that was now crowded with personnel, where most of the people gathered. The great chamber, a full cross-section of the research platform, had been at first a storage hold. At the mission's beginning eighty percent of the three-hundred-meter structure had been equipment and supplies; but as the immense stores were used and the holds became available, the crew had spread out from its original cramped quarters. Now the oceanic platform was little more than a floating laboratory.

Eyes lifted from the sonar displays to interrogate Dr. Ward; he met them with an impassive countenance, and announced quietly, "We've confirmed visual contact."

A nervous buzz arose; the director gestured for silence and went on, "They are still only shadows to the deep cameras. Dr. Isabel White has identified them—no more."

But this time the murmur was not to be settled. People pressed round the screens, peering into them as if with the naked eye they could pick out the shapes of reflected bioluminescence that were the Bathys, subjects of decades of research. They clasped each other's hands, embraced, spoke in urgent whispers. For the present their fears were forgotten and wonder prevailed.

Dr. Ward smiled grimly. The rest of the briefing he had been about to give didn't matter anyway, and it might have spoiled this moment.

He turned to go, and was halted by the sight of his colleague, standing at his elbow. His grim smile softened slightly; he asked, "How do you feel, Susan?"

Dr. Susan Holt drew an uncertain breath and released it in a faint sigh. "I don't know. It's remarkable that they're really coming up." She was thinking, he judged shrewdly, of the implications for bioethics and moral philosophy, subjects that had consumed their debates for months...

He said, with a touch of dry amusement, "What did you think might happen? After all, we've been monitoring them for thirty years."

"That's just it," said Susan shakily. "Thirty years of systematic observation—and we still don't understand their intentions. We don't know if they're coming as ambassadors or invaders..."

The director put a hand on her shoulder with reassuring pressure. "Don't worry. Whatever happens—we'll document it." But his face had hardened against registering the gnawing of that same doubtful fear within him. He let his hand fall. "I'd better get to the bridge. There are new protocols to implement now—for contact."

He left her and began to climb the stairway again. Someone dimmed the lights, and an awed whisper ran through the operations center as the people saw the first clear images appear on the screens, illuminated by the platform's own deep-sea floodlights. In that light Susan's eyes gleamed with scientific fascination and dread.

Director Ward found Lead Analyst Max Johnson looking as focused as he'd ever seen him. Max was finding that the actual observed patterns of the ascending formation agreed quite closely with his predictions from decades of acoustic data. He had already prepared a communication protocol based on information theory principles.

Ward nodded curt approval, remarking, "Probably they'll initiate contact before we do."

Max was jolted out of his concentration. "Uh, Director," he said hesitantly. "What kind of reception do you think they're planning?"

Ward shook his head slowly. "Who knows? We don't know whether any of the other Deep Survey missions made contact, or if they survived. And we don't know what changes have taken place in the abyss. It's possible—not likely, though—that something has happened to break the ecological continuity to the point where our presence has been misinterpreted as hostile."

He turned away tight-lipped and left the bridge. From his private office-cabin, he sent a message to Chief Biologist Isabel White to notify him as soon as the Bathys' morphology became clear; then he sat idle, alone with his thoughts.

The platform's automated systems had scant need of monitoring; Omar Ward found himself wishing that he could find some demanding task for everyone on board, himself included, to fill up the hours that remained.

There was an extensive digital library in the cabin, but he couldn't persuade himself to occupy time that way. He could go down and watch the screens, or to the residential section where he might find Susan and the other senior researchers—but somehow he didn't want to do that either.

He felt empty, drained—like the platform's research objectives. As the Meridian's mission goals and the hope of peaceful contact with an unknown intelligence had evolved, so the certainty had gone out of him. Now the final phase was beginning.

Perhaps, he thought, he was feeling the weight of his thirty years in deep-sea research—though physically he was only fifty-two now, fifteen years older than when this particular survey had begun. That was the toll of a career spent in isolated research stations, monitoring signals from the deep while years and decades had passed in the surface world.

Thoughtfully Ward got to his feet and stood surveying a cabinet with built-in recording equipment and storage for data archives. There were about three dozen digital files there—his personal logs of the great survey, a segment of his life and of scientific history. He might add that to the platform's official documentation and its collections of biological data, as a report to whatever authorities might be interested on the surface—if such authorities were still paying attention.

Ward selected a file from among the earliest. It was one he had made shortly after arriving at the Redwood Station in Orvandor, beginning of the first phase of the survey. He loaded it onto the player.

His own voice came from the speaker, fresher, more energetic and confident than he knew it was now.

"Day thirty-three of deep acoustic monitoring from Redwood Station, Orvandor.

"Our initial surveys of the Orvandor Trench drew unprecedented results. There are organized acoustic patterns, far too complex to be random geological activity, and unlike any known biological signatures.

"Our hopes were exceeded—and I think all of us, even remembering previous failed contact attempts, hoped more than we dared to admit. If the Orvandor signals possessed a decipherable pattern, we could establish communication within a few years of surface time.

"It is encouraging to note that the team seems only more determined. We continue monitoring; the signal complexity, so unlike surface communications, beckons. If success comes, a generation will have passed in research; colleagues, mentors, all the generation that launched the Deep Survey programs will have retired or passed away. Nevertheless we continue. Our generation's dream, humanity's dream, lives in us and in the mission forever..."

Presently Omar Ward switched off that younger voice of his and leaned back, an ironic smile touching his lips. That fervent idealism seemed remote and foreign to him now. The excitement of discovery must still have been fresh in his mind.

He rose, slipped the file back in its directory and selected another, later one.

"One month since we detected the coordinated movement patterns suggesting organized migration from deeper zones.

"We face the unsettling realization that what was feared is probably true—that intelligent life in the deep ocean is not only real but potentially vast in scale, and that we may have been observed far longer than we've been observing.

"It makes no difference, of course; we cannot abandon the mission... This may be humanity's best chance of establishing contact with a truly alien intelligence without space exploration. Certainly the construction of these deep-sea platforms and their support infrastructure, the immense expenditure of resources and international diplomacy that went into them, left several nations' budgets strained. Only once in a long age does humanity rise to such a collaborative effort—the effort of the International Space Station, or the global pandemic response of the early twenty-first century.

"Looked at historically, such cooperative outbursts are the result of humanity recognizing threats or opportunities that transcend national boundaries... In our era, the discovery of organized intelligence in the ocean depths was such a revelation—so we launched the Deep Surveys. Perhaps our effort will prove as futile as previous attempts at interspecies communication, less practical than simple ecosystem restoration... In any case, direct contact seems inevitable; but Earth could at least approach it with scientific documentation and protocols grounded in bioethics, expanding our understanding of consciousness itself...

"Hopeless, unless we understand their language!"

Omar Ward shook his head and removed the file. That was from the time when he had grown philosophical after the initial breakthroughs.

He selected one more file that was only two years old. The recorded voice carried a strange intensity...

"We are monitoring the deepest regions of the Foxwood Trench; hundreds of signals show on the acoustic arrays, each signal embedded in a complex harmonic structure like voices singing in vast cathedrals, for we are detecting what appears to be a civilization.

"According to our models, the Meridian has reached its optimal monitoring position. Now we wait for them to acknowledge our presence—but hope is small that any of our communication attempts will be understood, as have none of the thousands of signal patterns transmitted already.

"But what are a few thousand patterns in a language of potentially millions? We have only, as it were, learned a handful of words in an alien tongue, while the full complexity of their communication still remains far beyond our comprehension.

"On scientific grounds I have had Isabel White conduct morphological analyses using our deepest probes. There are structures down there in a volume of ocean where one finds only extremophile bacteria in most places; there if anywhere must exist the civilization we seek! But the deepest zones are eleven kilometers down...

"Even so—by deploying our remaining deep probes, the Meridian could achieve observations that would give us definitive answers. It would be a one-way deployment—even if enough probes remained, there would be little point in surface missions after potentially disturbing a civilization that has remained hidden for millennia.

"That was why the planners limited our survey to non-invasive methods. Even now, according to the risk management protocols established then, our presence—if they perceive us as hostile—could trigger a response that destabilizes the entire marine ecosystem.

"Why maintain distance, then, with the possibility of direct contact? Why not deploy all our resources and make definitive observations? What use is adherence to protocols thirty years old, whose makers are retired and which may be outdated?

"Would the crew support it? I don't know—some of them still show caution, though they know intellectually that this opportunity may never come again..."

The recording continued: "Today I gave orders to prepare for full probe deployment at dawn. We've waited long enough. This is why we came."

Omar Ward stopped the playback abruptly. He stared at the dark screen for a long moment, then pulled up a separate file—his mission log from the following day. He scanned the entry, his jaw tight.

The official record showed he had countermanded his own order before it could be executed. The probes remained in their bays. The aggressive deployment had never happened.

He remembered that morning vividly—waking before the scheduled launch, lying in his bunk staring at the ceiling panels, feeling the weight of thirty years pressing down on him. He had recorded that order in a moment of frustrated conviction, certain that bold action was finally justified. But in the quiet hours that followed, doubt had crept back in. The protocols existed for reasons. The ethical frameworks weren't obstacles to be discarded when inconvenient.

He had gone to the operations center and quietly canceled the deployment, telling the crew only that circumstances had changed. No one had questioned him. Perhaps they had been relieved.

Ward sighed heavily and leaned back in his chair. The fierce temptation he'd felt that night still troubled him—how close he'd come to abandoning everything he was supposed to represent. A phrase from an old poem came into his mind, something he'd read once about exploration and the cost of reaching too far...

He wondered if there would still be a quiet beach and a warm sunny place beside it where a research-weary man, relieved at last of responsibility, could rest and think no more... Those things went on, if people preserved them. And a forest where he and young researchers could go hiking, and lie on their backs at night and gaze at the stars, far away, so different from the abyss... He wasn't sure he would want to do that, though.

Suddenly a faint tremor went through the platform; it seemed to shudder one moment.

The director was on his feet instantly, but then his movements became measured. Whatever it had been was past, and he had a good idea what it had been—a pressure wave, nothing unusual in the vicinity of large marine organisms, though in the open ocean such impacts were rare. No harm could have been done. The Meridian's stabilization systems were sophisticated and reliable.

Just as he reached for the door control, the emergency comm shrilled imperatively. Omar Ward turned, frowning—surely a pressure wave wasn't that serious. Coincidence, maybe—it might be Isabel White calling as instructed.

He reached the comm at the moment when another, heavier impact shook the platform. Ward grabbed the receiver quickly.

"Director?" It was Max Johnson's voice, tense. "Director, we're under attack!"

"Activate emergency protocols. All stations." He had said it automatically, then felt a curious detached relief at the knowledge that after all these years he could still respond decisively to a crisis. There was a moment's silence, and he heard the alarm start—three short tones and repeat, sounding through all the sections of the research platform. Knowing that Max was still there, he said, "Now—attacked by what?"

"Creatures," said Max helplessly. "Dozens of them so far. No, there are more now." Repeated impacts shuddered the Meridian's framework. The analyst said, obviously striving for calm, "They're large organisms, perhaps twenty meters long, but they move with purpose. The sonar barely tracked them before they started ramming us. Can't get clear images long enough to classify them."

"If they're biological," said Omar Ward deliberately, "they can't generate enough force to breach our hull. Hold position. I'll be right there."

In the corridor he nearly collided with a young researcher. Leo Hernández's eyes were wide; he had heard the director's words.

"Something's happening," he said with earnest seriousness and, without wasting time on questions, "Can I help, Dr. Ward?"

Ward hesitated, said, "All right. Come along and stay clear of the equipment." He headed for the operations center with strides that the young man matched easily.

There were people moving quickly in the corridors, heading for their stations. Their faces were set, frightened, confused. The Meridian shuddered, again and again, under impacts that must have had tremendous force behind them; but it held its position above the trench, its stabilization systems compensating.

To a person, the platform's senior staff were already in operations, most of them breathless. To a person they looked to Director Omar Ward.

"Well?" he said sharply. "What's their behavior?"

Max Johnson spoke. "There are at least forty of them now, sir, and they're all targeting structural weak points."

The director stared into the dark sonar display where occasional bright shapes appeared ominously, never in the same position twice.

Leo pressed himself against the wall and watched silently. His young face showed more curiosity than fear; he had confidence in the director.

"If they had greater mass," reasoned the director, "they'd have used it by now. They're trying to disable us. But at this rate, they can't breach the hull as long as our systems function—or until they bring up something larger."

The impacts continued—whether from physical rams or some form of biological discharge would be hard to determine and it didn't matter; whatever was hitting the Meridian's hull was doing so with coordinated precision.

But that hull was strong. It was designed to withstand the pressures of the deep ocean and the forces of major storms; impacts from outside were absorbed by the structure's flexibility and the stabilization field's dampening effect. A large organism, on striking it, would be repelled—possibly injured by the impact—and the platform, in obedience to physics, would shift too, but since its mass was anchored and stabilized, its displacement was minimal.

The people in the Meridian would have felt nothing at all of the sustained assault being directed against them, save that their stabilization systems were intentionally calibrated to allow some movement to provide feedback to the crew.

One of the scientists said shakily, "It's as if they've been preparing for this. But why would they—"

"That," said the director grimly, "is what we have to find out. Why they're attacking. At least, I suspect we'll learn soon."

The Meridian held steadily in position, maintaining its monitoring stance. Even if one were inclined to retreat, there seemed no reason to abandon station or change protocols. There was nowhere else to go and too much invested if there had been; come what might, this was the mission's critical moment—perhaps in a more confrontational way than had been anticipated. All around moved the attacking organisms, circling, coordinating, and striking, always striking, with the focused intensity of a defended territory. The research platform bore no weapons—but suddenly on one of the sonar displays a bright shape flared and then went dark.

Leo exclaimed in surprise and then fell silent, but no one was paying attention to him. The people in the Meridian's operations center looked questions at each other, as the thought of internal conflict flashed into many minds at once. But Director Ward said soberly, "It must have collided with another. Maybe its own momentum, if it struck at the wrong angle."

He studied the data accumulated so far. A few unclear images had been captured, which showed elongated organisms much like known deep-sea species, except that they displayed coordinated behavior and far greater size. Their size was difficult to ascertain, because you needed to know their distance and velocity—but sonar echoes gave the distance, and likewise, by the Doppler method, the speed of directly approaching or receding organisms. It was apparent that the attacking creatures were even larger than Max had initially estimated—too large to be individuals. Massive, purposeful beings with devastating impact force.

"Coordinated behavior, certainly," said Omar Ward, but a chill ran down his spine as it occurred to him that perhaps the attackers represented a defensive response to perceived invasion. They had seen no comparable intelligence in the ocean depths they had explored, but the Bathys might have been monitoring them far longer than suspected and decided humanity was a threat.

It became evident, too, that the assault was being sustained by waves of fresh attackers, while others retreated into the deep, presumably to rest or receive new instructions. That argued a planned and organized defense with serious purpose behind it.

Dr. Susan Holt, the bioethics specialist, said quietly, "At the rate we're sustaining damage, the hull integrity will be compromised in twelve to eighteen hours."

"We should reach the surface before then," Max said hopefully.

"If they don't escalate their attack first."

Leo spoke up suddenly, his voice carrying across the tense room. "Director Ward, we should deploy the deep probes now—get definitive observations while we still can. This opportunity may never come again!"

Several heads turned toward the young researcher. His eyes were bright with the conviction of someone who had spent his career dreaming of this moment. "The protocols are thirty years old," he continued urgently. "The people who wrote them have retired. Why should we be bound by constraints that may be completely outdated?"

Ward studied the young man's face—so familiar, that expression. He had seen it in his own mirror, years ago. He had recorded those very arguments himself, in the dark hours when patience seemed like cowardice and bold action like wisdom.

"The protocols exist because our presence could trigger exactly this kind of response," Ward said quietly. "Perhaps already has."

"But we're already under attack!" Leo pressed. "What's left to protect? We should at least—"

"No." The word came out harder than Ward intended. He softened his tone. "The mission parameters are clear. We observe. We document. We don't provoke."

Leo looked ready to argue further, but something in the director's expression stopped him. The young researcher fell silent, though his frustration was evident.

"We're under a strategic disadvantage," said the director, turning back to the displays, "of not knowing their motivation."

Leo's voice came again, this time more measured. "But we have an advantage too."

His director raised an eyebrow. "What's that? I don't see it."

"They're defending and we're not threatening," said the young researcher. Then, seeing he hadn't made himself clear, "In any conflict, if one side misunderstands the other's intentions, communication can resolve it."

Thoughtful expressions appeared on several faces. Director Ward said, "Maybe you're right. They do seem to be defensive. But we're not in a position to prove our intentions." He turned back to the others. "As I was going to suggest—I think we should attempt communication with them. At least we may discover what triggered this response."

And now instead of passive monitoring the platform was broadcasting on multiple frequencies, cycling through various patterns, repeating on each the same recorded message based on information theory principles:

"We are peaceful observers. We mean no harm. We are the research mission Meridian from the surface world..." And so on, identifying themselves and explaining that they were unarmed and scientific, that there must be some misunderstanding, and asking, "What do you want?"

There was no answer. The platform held position, its systems managing the assault. Those outside were expending vastly greater energy in the effort to drive them away, but maintaining structural integrity was taxing the Meridian's resources too. Once more Omar Ward had the insidious sense of his own resolve weakening along with his platform's defenses.

Isabel White approached him urgently. "If you have time, Director—I've got analysis on the organisms now."

Eagerly Ward took the data compilation from the biological scans. But it told him little; only the basic morphology was clear, and that was unlike anything in the databases... He looked up questioningly at Isabel White.

"There are some disturbing features," said the biologist carefully. "First of all—they show signs of artificial modification. And in their behavior patterns, our best analysis should reveal instinctive responses—but it does not.

"The coordination you see is too precise. It indicates communication systems less than one millisecond in latency—so their nervous systems can't be simple neural networks, but must involve something more sophisticated, perhaps bioengineered enhancement."

"Is that all?" demanded Ward.

"Isn't it enough?" said Isabel blankly. "Well—we tried biochemical analysis, of course. The samples show nothing unusual in basic composition, but the complexity science models indicate designed systems."

The director sighed. "Good work," he said. "Continue analysis; perhaps you can explain these anomalies before—"

"We know who you are," interrupted a resonant voice with strange harmonics, "and your explanations are insufficient."

Omar Ward turned sharply to the communications station, his weariness vanishing. He said quickly, "Then tell us what we've done wrong," and the words overlapped absurdly with the same plea in the still-repeating broadcast.

He cut off the recording; as he did so the speaker, still carrying deep harmonic undertones, said, "It may interest you to know that you are not the first. The two other deep research missions that descended have already been expelled, as you will soon be—the sooner, if you continue your intrusion."

Omar Ward's mind was working rapidly. The voice—which must be coming from the deep, transmitted somehow by the organisms—was revealing things perhaps unintentionally: that it had responded at all suggested uncertainty, he deduced from the fact it had chosen to communicate, and from its last statement he gathered that the Meridian's steadfast position and continued monitoring had somehow concerned it. So it was trying to drive them away.

He filed those observations for consideration. Just now he had to know something, so urgently that he asked it directly, "Are you the Bathys we've been studying?"

The voice carried a tone of cold amusement. "We are the Bathys," it answered, "but you are intruders."

The director was momentarily silent, searching for an adequate response. Behind him somebody gasped, the only sound in the stunned silence, and the platform shuddered slightly as another massive impact struck its hull.

"Suppose we discuss this misunderstanding," said Omar Ward steadily. He specified a visual communication frequency compatible with their systems.

"Very well." The tone suggested reluctant agreement. The voice continued in its language that was perfectly intelligible but strange-sounding with its harmonic complexity. "Perhaps, if you understand your violation, you will follow the prudent example of the Bayview mission's leader."

Omar Ward tensed. The Bayview Station in Selvoria, established to monitor the southern trenches, had been the most advanced of the research platforms—and its director had been a respected colleague of Ward's... He said carefully, "What happened to them?"

"They resisted our warnings, which surround you now, for some time," said the voice with disturbing calm. "When they understood it was futile, they chose withdrawal over confrontation, and returned to the surface." A brief pause. "The visual connection is ready."

Omar Ward activated the screen at the specified frequency, and an image formed there. The face that appeared was humanoid in structure, but profoundly modified. The features showed the same basic bilateral symmetry possessed by surface humans, but there was an unmistakable quality of adaptive redesign. Most obviously, the eyes seemed designed for low-light conditions, and the skin showed translucent qualities.

The being regarded Omar Ward with an expression of stern assessment. "Have you any other questions before you depart?"

"Yes," said Ward with controlled intensity. "You haven't explained one thing. Why do you consider our research a violation? You can see we're conducting scientific observation."

The modified human studied him with a calculating look in those adapted eyes, behind which the director glimpsed something like protective determination.

"It is enough for you to know that you must leave our territory."

Ward felt the familiar pull—the urge to push harder, to demand answers, to deploy every resource at his disposal and force the truth from the depths. Thirty years of patience straining against this moment. He thought of his recorded order, the one he had canceled. He thought of Leo's eager face, echoing his own younger convictions.

He took a slow breath and said only, "We will consider your request."

The screen went dark. Around him, the operations center was silent except for the distant thuds of the continuing assault. Ward stood motionless, his hands clasped behind his back, staring at nothing.
